questions.question_text: How many real solutions does $x^{2}+5x+4=0$ have?

options.why: Read $\Delta=9$ as $\Delta=0$; a positive discriminant gives two solutions, not one.
Computed $b^{2}+4ac=25+16=41$ with the wrong sign, or slipped $\Delta$ negative; $\Delta=25-16=9>0$.

questions.solution_text:
$a=1,\ b=5,\ c=4$
$\Delta=5^{2}-4(1)(4)$
$=25-16$
$=9$
$\Delta>0$, so the equation has two real solutions.

questions.question_text: How many real solutions does $x^{2}-8x+16=0$ have?

options.why: Assumed a quadratic always has two solutions without checking that $\Delta=64-64=0$.
Computed $\Delta=b^{2}+4ac=64+64=128$ or slipped the sign so $\Delta$ looked negative; here $\Delta=0$.

questions.solution_text:
$a=1,\ b=-8,\ c=16$
$\Delta=(-8)^{2}-4(1)(16)$
$=64-64$
$=0$
$\Delta=0$, so the equation has one real solution.

questions.question_text: How many real solutions does $x^{2}+3x+7=0$ have?

options.why: Computed $\Delta=b^{2}+4ac=9+28=37$, flipping the sign of the $4ac$ term; correctly $\Delta=9-28=-19<0$.
Treated a negative discriminant as if it were zero; $\Delta<0$ means no real solutions, not one.

questions.solution_text:
$a=1,\ b=3,\ c=7$
$\Delta=3^{2}-4(1)(7)$
$=9-28$
$=-19$
$\Delta<0$, so the equation has no real solutions.

options.why: Assumed $\Delta=20$ is a perfect square; $20$ lies between $16$ and $25$, so the solutions are irrational.
Read $\Delta=20$ as $\Delta=0$; a positive discriminant gives two distinct solutions.
Made a sign slip in $36-4(1)(4)$; correctly $\Delta=36-16=20>0$.

questions.solution_text:
$a=1,\ b=-6,\ c=4$
$\Delta=(-6)^{2}-4(1)(4)$
$=36-16$
$=20$
$\Delta>0$ but $20$ is not a perfect square, so there are two distinct irrational solutions.

options.why: Did not recognise $289=17^{2}$ as a perfect square, so the rational solutions were called irrational.
Computed $\Delta=169-4(5)(6)=49$, dropping the minus sign on $c=-6$; correctly $\Delta=169+120=289$.
Read $\Delta=289$ as $\Delta=0$; a positive discriminant gives two distinct solutions.

questions.solution_text:
$a=5,\ b=13,\ c=-6$
$\Delta=13^{2}-4(5)(-6)$
$=169+120$
$=289$
$\Delta>0$ and $289=17^{2}$ is a perfect square, so there are two distinct rational solutions.

questions.question_text:
A quadratic equation has discriminant $\Delta=-9$.
Describe its solutions.

options.why: Treated $-9$ as if it were positive; a negative discriminant gives no real solutions.
Confused $\Delta<0$ with $\Delta=0$; only $\Delta=0$ gives a single real solution.

questions.solution_text:
$\Delta=-9$
$\Delta<0$, so there are no real solutions.

questions.question_text:
A quadratic equation has discriminant $\Delta=81$.
Describe its solutions.

options.why: Did not recognise $81=9^{2}$ as a perfect square, so the rational solutions were called irrational.
Read $\Delta=81$ as $\Delta=0$; a positive discriminant gives two distinct solutions.
Treated the discriminant as negative; $81>0$ so there are real solutions.

questions.solution_text:
$\Delta=81$
$\Delta>0$ and $81$ is a perfect square, so there are two distinct rational solutions.

options.why: Assumed $\Delta=40$ is a perfect square; $40$ lies between $36$ and $49$, so the solutions are irrational.
Used $c=3$ without rearranging to $2x^{2}-8x+3=0$, or slipped a sign; $\Delta=64-24=40>0$.
Read $\Delta=40$ as $\Delta=0$; a positive discriminant gives two distinct solutions.

questions.solution_text:
$2x^{2}+3=8x$
$2x^{2}-8x+3=0$
$a=2,\ b=-8,\ c=3$
$\Delta=(-8)^{2}-4(2)(3)$
$=64-24$
$=40$
$\Delta>0$ but $40$ is not a perfect square, so there are two distinct irrational solutions.

options.why: Did not recognise $169=13^{2}$ as a perfect square, so the rational solutions were called irrational.
Rearranged to $6x^{2}-5x+6=0$ instead of $6x^{2}-5x-6=0$, giving $\Delta=25-144<0$; correctly $\Delta=25+144=169$.
Read $\Delta=169$ as $\Delta=0$; a positive discriminant gives two distinct solutions.

questions.solution_text:
$6x^{2}=5x+6$
$6x^{2}-5x-6=0$
$a=6,\ b=-5,\ c=-6$
$\Delta=(-5)^{2}-4(6)(-6)$
$=25+144$
$=169$
$\Delta>0$ and $169=13^{2}$ is a perfect square, so there are two distinct rational solutions.

questions.question_text: For $f(x)=3x^2-9x+12$, how many solutions are there to $f(x)=0$?

options.why: The discriminant is not zero, so there is no repeated real root.
The discriminant $81-144$ is negative, not positive.
The quadratic coefficients determine the discriminant completely.

questions.solution_text: The discriminant is $(-9)^2-4(3)(12)=81-144=-63<0$. Therefore the quadratic has no real solutions.
